pages.title: Welcome to the Machine Learning(ML) course!
pages.content:
Get ready to dive into the exciting world of Machine Learning - where data meets intelligence, and possibilities are endless.



**Prerequisites:** 
Before you start, you should be comfortable with: 
[Python Programming](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/python-development/), [Pandas](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/pandas) for data manipulation and [NumPy](https://www.codechef.com/learn/course/numpy) for numerical operations

---

**How This Course Works**
- **Bite-sized lessons** designed to be easy to follow at your own pace
- **Real-world use cases** to help you understand where and why ML matters
- **Visual explanations** and simplified concepts to make learning fun
- **Mini-projects and code examples** you can try, tweak, and apply
- **Progressive learning flow** - starting from basics and moving toward hands-on model building

**By the end of this course, you will:**



 - Understand what Machine Learning is and how it differs from AI and Deep Learning
 - Learn how ML is used in real-world sectors like healthcare, finance, retail, and more
 - Explore core ML tasks like classification, regression, clustering, and recommendation systems
 - Build your first ML model from collecting data to making predictions
 - Discover how to evaluate and improve your models for better accuracy
 - Get hands-on with practical examples using simple, beginner-friendly tools






Let’s make Machine Learning simple, exciting, and useful - together.

**Click “Next” to begin your ML journey.**

pages.title: Introduction to Machine Learning
pages.content:
- So what is **Machine Learning (ML)**? It is a part of **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** that builds systems which can **learn from data** and **improve over time**, without being explicitly programmed for every rule. 
- ML uses **past data** to make **predictions or decisions** on **new, unseen data**.

---

**How It Works**





**Think of it like teaching a computer with examples. Instead of writing every rule, we give it past data, and it figures out the rules by itself.**

pages.title: Can you predict the next data
pages.content:
Before diving deeper, let’s try a simple exercise.

---

**Problem Statement**

We collected data of students’ **study hours** and their **exam marks**:

| Study Hours | Marks |
|-------------|-------|
| 1 | 40 |
| 2 | 50 |
| 3 | 60 |
| 4 | 70 |

**Q: If a new student studies for 5 hours, what marks do you think they’ll get?**

---

**Key Takeaway**

For this small dataset, the pattern is easy to see. 
But in real life: 
- Data can be noisy (not perfectly increasing). 
- There may be many features (study hours, sleep, attendance, etc.). 
- Relationships can be nonlinear or hidden. 

That’s why we use different **machine learning algorithms** to automatically discover these patterns for us.

pages.title: When patterns gets complicated
pages.content:
In real life, data is often **messy** and has **multiple factors** affecting the outcome. Let’s see an example.

---

**Example: Predicting Exam Marks with Multiple Features**

| Study Hours | Sleep Hours | Attendance | Marks |
|-------------|------------|-----------|-------|
| 1 | 6 | 80% | 45 |
| 2 | 5 | 90% | 50 |
| 3 | 7 | 85% | 65 |
| 4 | 6 | 70% | 68 |
| 5 | 4 | 95% | 72 |

Can you predict the marks for a new student just by looking at the table? 

---

**Why It’s Harder**

- There are many things that matter at the same time (study hours, sleep, attendance).
- The data does not follow a simple straight-line trend.
- Some factors may affect each other (for example, both very little sleep and too much sleep can reduce marks).
---

**How Machine Learning Helps**

- ML algorithms can study past data and discover patterns automatically.
- They can handle:
 - Many different inputs at once (like hours, sleep, attendance).
 - Messy or missing data.
 - Complicated relationships that humans can’t spot easily.

pages.title: Different Ways Machines Can Learn
pages.content:
- So far, we’ve seen that machines can find **patterns** in data. But here’s an interesting question:
- Do all problems look the same?
- Will a machine always learn in the same way?
 - The answer is **No**.
Just like humans, machines also have **different ways of learning**, depending on what kind of information they get.

---

**Imagine three kids trying to learn something new:**





- Kid A learns best when a teacher gives the question and the correct answer.
- Kid B has no teacher, but loves grouping things that “look alike.”
- Kid C learns by trying things out and improving from mistakes.

**They all learn differently. But which style belongs to machine learning?**

pages.title: Supervised Learning
pages.content:
- Remember Kid A from our analogy? They had a **teacher correcting them** after every attempt.
That’s exactly what **Supervised Learning** is in machine learning.
- In supervised learning, the model is trained on a labeled dataset.
For example: Carrot, Tomato, Bell Pepper.
 - This means that for every input (the picture of a vegetable), the correct answer (the name of the vegetable) is already provided.
- The goal is for the model to **learn the mapping** between inputs (features) and outputs (labels), so it can make accurate predictions on new, unseen data.



---

**In the image above, we have a dataset of vegetables with labels (Carrot, Tomato, Bell Pepper). The model uses these labeled examples to learn. Later, when we give new vegetable images, it can correctly identify and classify the vegetables.**

pages.title: Our Dataset & Training Process
pages.content:
Let’s imagine we collected fruit samples with their **weight** and **sweetness**.

| Weight (g) | Sweetness (1–10) | Fruit (Label) |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ------------- |
| 150 | 8 | Apple |
| 170 | 7 | Apple |
| 130 | 9 | Apple |
| 200 | 4 | Orange |
| 220 | 3 | Orange |
| 210 | 5 | Orange |

- Here, each row is one training example.
- The **features** are weight & sweetness.
- The **label** is whether the fruit is Apple or Orange.

---

**What does "training" mean?**

* Training means we show the model lots of examples.
* The model looks for **patterns** in the features that match with the correct label.
* After enough examples, it can **generalize** to predict new fruits it has never seen.

---

**Example Thought Experiment**

Imagine a new fruit comes in:

- Weight = 160g, Sweetness = 8
Our model (after training) will look at past data and say:
“Hmm, this looks more like the Apples I’ve seen before.”
- So, the prediction will be: **Apple**

pages.title: Unsupervised Learning - Introduction
pages.content:
Before exploring **unsupervised learning**, let's see why we need it.

- In **supervised learning**, we already know the output (like gender), so the model just learns patterns based on examples.
- But what if we **don’t have the output labels**?
- That’s where **unsupervised learning** comes in. **Unsupervised Learning:**
It is a type of machine learning where the model is given **data without any labels**, and it tries to **find patterns, groupings, or structures** on its own.

---

**Example: Grouping Toys**

Imagine we have three types of toys: **cars**, **teddy bears**, and **Legos**.




We can group them so that:

* All cars are in **one group**
* All teddy bears in **another group**
* All Legos in **a third group**

This way, toys of the same type are **automatically grouped together**.

pages.title: Reinforcement Learning - Introduction
pages.content:
- So, just like we’ve explored **supervised** and **unsupervised** learning, now let’s ask:

**Why do we even need **reinforcement learning**? What’s missing that it brings to the table?**

---

**Why Do We Need Reinforcement Learning?** 




Let’s say we’re training a **robot** or an **AI game agent**.

* We **don’t have labeled data** (like supervised learning).
* We can’t group anything (like unsupervised learning).
* Instead:
 * The agent **tries actions** (e.g., move left/right).
 * It gets **feedback** in the form of a **reward or penalty**.
 * It **learns by trial and error** → just like **humans learn from experience**.

**What is Reinforcement Learning?**
A type of machine learning where an **agent learns by performing actions** and receiving **rewards or punishments** from its environment.

---

 
 Fun Fact: You've just stepped into one of the core pillars of AI and Deep Learning.

practiceProblems.title: Unsupervised Learning- Worked Example
practiceProblems.description:
We’ll see **how unsupervised learning groups fruits** using a simple dataset.

**Dataset**

| Weight (g) | Color Score |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 150 | 8 |
| 160 | 7 |
| 200 | 3 |
| 210 | 4 |

**We **don’t provide fruit types** (Apple/Orange) — the model discovers groups on its own.**

---

**Step-by-Step Explanation**

1. **Create the model** → we use **KMeans clustering**, a simple algorithm that groups similar points.
2. **Train the model** → the model looks at the features (weight & color score) and finds **patterns to form clusters**.
3. **Predict clusters** → the model assigns a cluster number to each fruit.

**Don’t worry about the internal mechanics** — focus on understanding how the model **groups similar fruits together**.

---

**Key Points**

* The model **learns groupings automatically**.
* Fruits with **similar weight & color** end up in the same cluster.
* You **don’t need labels** — that’s what makes it unsupervised.

practiceProblems.description:
- Now it’s your turn to **apply unsupervised learning**!
- We have a dataset of fruits with **weight (grams)** and **color score (1–10)**.

| Weight (g) | Color Score |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 150 | 8 |
| 160 | 7 |
| 200 | 3 |
| 210 | 4 |

**Notice: We **don’t provide fruit types**. The model has to discover groups on its own.**

---

**Your Task**

1. Use **unsupervised learning** to **group the fruits into clusters**.
2. Predict which cluster each fruit belongs to.
3. **Don’t worry about the internal mechanics** — focus on understanding how the model **groups similar fruits together**.

---


**What You Need to Do**

* Complete the missing lines of code.
* Fit the KMeans model to the dataset.
* Predict cluster assignments for all fruits.

---

**Expected Output**

After completing the code, running it should print something like:

```sdbkf
Cluster assignments: [0 0 1 1]
```
